page: Vultr vc2-1c-0.5gb belongs to the Cloud Compute family and operates on an entry-level x86_64 architecture. The server provisions 1 shared vCPU backed by an Intel processor alongside 0.5 GB of system memory. Hardware resources are bundled with 10 GB of local NVMe SSD storage and include one complimentary public IPv4 address. The configuration contains no discrete graphics accelerators.

The shared allocation of the single Intel vCPU implies that compute cycles share physical resources across hypervisor tenants, making throughput variable under sustained compute loads. Memory capacity is constrained to 0.5 GB, which restricts the execution of memory-intensive application stacks and multi-process runtimes. However, the integration of local NVMe SSD storage provides responsive solid-state read and write operations directly attached to the virtual machine. From an infrastructure cost perspective, the minimal resource profile delivers an economical entry point for operational tasks where dedicated processing cores are unnecessary.

Given the single shared core and half-gigabyte memory boundary, the vc2-1c-0.5gb is tailored for utility tasks and low-overhead services. Common deployment scenarios include lightweight reverse proxies, minimal DNS servers, small VPN gateways, health-check monitoring agents, low-traffic static websites, and ephemeral development or testing instances.
description: Vultr vc2-1c-0.5gb is an entry-tier virtual server within the Cloud Compute lineup, configured with an x86_64 Intel processor. It delivers 1 shared vCPU paired with 0.5 GB of system RAM, 10 GB of bundled local NVMe SSD storage, and a single complimentary public IPv4 address. The server includes no hardware GPU acceleration. Compute capacity relies on a shared core model, which introduces susceptibility to resource contention under continuous processing demands. The 0.5 GB memory footprint restricts runtime environments to minimal daemon footprints and compact system configurations. Bundled NVMe storage provides solid-state disk latency, offering reasonable I/O capability relative to the compact footprint. Qualitatively, the small allocation presents a highly cost-efficient tier for resource-lean deployments where dedicated physical cores are unnecessary. Suitable use cases comprise basic network utilities, DNS hosting, lightweight reverse proxies, personal testing environments, and low-footprint background automation scripts.
